cards.title: The Software Supply Chain
cards.teaser: Your application is not just the code you wrote — it is every dependency you pulled, every build tool you ran, every CI job that touched the artifact, and every registry that hosted it. Attackers know this. Most developers do not.

runs.text: The
software supply chain
is the complete set of components, processes, and people involved in producing and delivering software. It includes everything upstream of your running binary:

items.text: — the code your team wrote, including version control history and contributor identities.

— open-source packages pulled from npm, PyPI, Maven, RubyGems, and other registries. A typical Node.js application has 800–1,000 transitive dependencies; a Python ML project can have several thousand.
— compilers, bundlers, linters, code generators, and CI runners that transform source into artifacts. Each tool is itself a supply-chain component.
— base images, OS packages, environment variables, and secrets available during the build. A compromised base image poisons every artifact built from it.
— artifact registries, CDNs, and update servers that carry your artifact to its destination. Compromise here affects every consumer.

runs.text: The fundamental insight of supply-chain security is that
any link in this chain can be compromised

. An attacker who cannot break your application directly may succeed by subverting a dependency, a build step, or a distribution channel. The perimeter model — secure the app, trust everything else — fails completely against this threat.

A 2021 Sonatype report found a 650% year-over-year increase in supply-chain attacks. The attack surface grew as open-source adoption accelerated and teams automated dependency management without implementing equivalent controls.

Your app is not just your code — it is every package you imported, every tool that built it, and every server that hosted it. Attackers target the weakest link in that entire chain, not necessarily your code itself.

cards.title: Landmark Supply-Chain Breaches
cards.teaser: SolarWinds (2020), Codecov (2021), and xz-utils (2024) are not cautionary tales about exotic attacks — they are demonstrations of the same pattern: trust the upstream artifact, get the upstream attacker.

runs.text: Three incidents define the modern supply-chain threat landscape:

items.text: Nation-state attackers (Cozy Bear / APT29) compromised the SolarWinds Orion build pipeline and injected a backdoor — SUNBURST — into signed software updates. Approximately 18,000 organizations installed the malicious update, including US federal agencies. The artifact was signed by SolarWinds' own certificate, so signature verification offered no protection.

Attackers compromised the Codecov Bash uploader script hosted on codecov.io. Any CI pipeline that curled and executed the script (a common pattern) exfiltrated environment variables — including AWS keys, GitHub tokens, and other secrets — to an attacker-controlled server. Over 29,000 organizations used Codecov at the time.

A multi-year social engineering attack. The attacker "JiaT75" spent approximately two years contributing legitimately to xz-utils, building trust, eventually becoming a maintainer. They then added a backdoor to the build system (not the source), targeting SSH authentication via systemd on select Linux distributions. Discovered accidentally by a Microsoft engineer before wide distribution.

The popular npm package event-stream (2M+ weekly downloads) was transferred to a new maintainer who added a malicious dependency (flatmap-stream) designed to steal Bitcoin wallets from a specific application (Copay). The attack targeted a downstream consumer, not all users — demonstrating targeted supply-chain attacks.

runs.text: The common pattern: attackers target the build pipeline, the distribution mechanism, or the maintainer identity — not the running application. Each breach exploited implicit trust: "this artifact came from the right place, therefore it is safe."

SolarWinds demonstrated that even signed software is not trustworthy if the signing key or build pipeline is compromised. Signatures prove provenance only when the signing infrastructure itself is secure.

SolarWinds: malware baked into a signed update. Codecov: a CI helper script that stole your secrets. xz-utils: a patient attacker who became a trusted maintainer. All three worked by subverting trust in the supply chain, not by breaking the application.

cards.title: SBOM — Software Bill of Materials
cards.teaser: An SBOM is an inventory of every component in your software: packages, versions, licenses, and provenance. Without it, you cannot answer "are we affected?" when the next Log4Shell drops.

runs.text: A
Software Bill of Materials (SBOM)

is a formal, machine-readable record of the components that make up a software artifact. Modeled on manufacturing BOMs, an SBOM answers: what is in this software, where did it come from, and under what license?
An SBOM typically records for each component:

items.text: — the package identifier and the exact version included.
that uniquely identifies the component across ecosystems.
— cryptographic digests (SHA-256) of the component for integrity verification.
— the SPDX license identifier (MIT, Apache-2.0, GPL-3.0) for license compliance.
— which components depend on which others, forming the full dependency graph.

runs.text: The Log4Shell vulnerability (CVE-2021-44228) illustrated SBOM's operational value. Organizations with SBOMs could query them to identify affected systems within hours. Organizations without them spent days manually auditing repositories. The US Executive Order 14028 (May 2021) subsequently mandated SBOM generation for software sold to the federal government, accelerating industry adoption.

SBOM generation is increasingly automated: Syft, CycloneDX CLI, and GitHub's dependency graph can produce SBOMs as part of a CI pipeline. The goal is continuous, automatic SBOM generation tied to every release artifact.

An SBOM is a complete ingredient list for your software. When a vulnerability hits, you check the SBOM instead of manually hunting through hundreds of repositories to find out whether you are affected.

cards.title: CycloneDX vs SPDX — SBOM Formats
cards.teaser: CycloneDX and SPDX are the two dominant SBOM standards. They solve the same problem with different emphases: SPDX prioritizes license compliance; CycloneDX prioritizes security and vulnerability management.

runs.text: Two standards dominate the SBOM ecosystem:

items.text: — originated at the Linux Foundation in 2010, became ISO/IEC 5962:2021. Originally designed for license compliance tracking. SPDX documents can be expressed in tag-value, JSON, RDF, or YAML formats. Widely used in open-source compliance tooling (FOSSA, Black Duck). The SPDX license list is the de facto standard for license identifiers across the industry.

— originated at OWASP in 2017. Security-first design: native support for vulnerability disclosure (VEX — Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange), dependency graph representation, attestation metadata, and formula components (build tooling). Supported formats: XML, JSON. Tooling integrations: Syft, Grype, Dependency-Track, Trivy.

runs.text: Practical comparison:

items.text: when license compliance is the primary concern, or when the consumer expects SPDX (e.g., many government procurement requirements specify SPDX).
when the primary use case is vulnerability management, continuous monitoring, or integration with security tooling.
are machine-readable and can be converted between each other using tools like
. Organizations with mixed requirements often generate both.

runs.text: CycloneDX's VEX (Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange) extension is particularly useful: it allows software producers to assert whether a known CVE is exploitable in their specific product configuration, reducing alert fatigue for consumers.

SPDX came from the license-compliance world; CycloneDX came from the security world. Both describe what is in your software, but CycloneDX has richer support for vulnerability tracking while SPDX has deeper license tooling.

cards.title: SLSA Framework — Supply-Chain Levels
cards.teaser: SLSA (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts) is a framework from Google that defines four levels of build integrity assurance. Level 1 generates provenance; Level 4 requires hermetic, reproducible builds with two-party review.

runs.text: SLSA (pronounced "salsa") defines a graduated set of requirements for build integrity. It answers the question: how confident can a consumer be that this artifact was produced from the claimed source through the claimed process?
The four levels (SLSA v1.0):

items.text: — the build process generates provenance (a document describing how the artifact was built: source, builder, build steps). Provenance need not be signed. Establishes a baseline; does not prevent tampering.

— provenance is signed by the build service (not the developer). Source is version-controlled. Builds run on a hosted, not developer-owned, build platform. Protects against individual developer compromise.

— the build service itself is audited and hardened. Source is retained (not mutable). Build runs in an isolated environment. Build instructions are defined in source. Protects against build-service compromise.

— hermetic builds (all inputs declared and resolved; no network access during build). Two-party review of all source changes. Reproducible builds (same inputs always produce bit-for-bit identical output). Provides the strongest assurance currently practical.

runs.text: Most organizations start at Level 1 (generate provenance from CI) and incrementally move toward Level 2 or 3. Level 4 is aspirational for most teams but achievable in constrained build environments. Major package ecosystems (PyPI, npm, Maven Central) are progressively requiring SLSA Level 2 or higher for published packages.

GitHub Actions supports SLSA Level 2 provenance generation natively via the slsa-framework/slsa-github-generator action. Running it produces a signed SLSA provenance attestation alongside your artifact without additional infrastructure.

SLSA is a checklist with four levels of build trustworthiness. Level 1 just writes down how the artifact was built. Level 4 proves it with signed, reproducible, hermetically sealed builds reviewed by two people.

cards.title: Sigstore — Keyless Signing Infrastructure
cards.teaser: Sigstore is an open-source project that makes artifact signing practical by eliminating the need to manage long-lived private keys. It uses short-lived certificates tied to OIDC identity and an immutable transparency log.

runs.text: Traditional artifact signing required managing a long-lived private key: generating it, storing it securely, rotating it, and revoking it when compromised. This operational burden caused most teams to skip signing entirely.
Sigstore
(sigstore.dev), a project under the OpenSSF, solves this with keyless signing.
Sigstore has three core components:

items.text: — issues short-lived (10-minute) code-signing certificates. To obtain a certificate, the signer authenticates with an OIDC provider (GitHub Actions, Google, Microsoft, GitHub user account). The certificate binds the signing key to the signer's identity (e.g., a GitHub Actions workflow URL). After signing, the private key can be discarded.

— an immutable, append-only public log of all signing events. When you sign an artifact, an entry is appended to Rekor containing the certificate, the artifact digest, and a timestamp. This log is Merkle-tree-backed; entries cannot be deleted or altered without detection.
— the CLI and Go library for interacting with the Sigstore ecosystem: signing artifacts, verifying signatures, attaching attestations, and querying Rekor.

runs.text: The keyless flow: authenticate with OIDC → Fulcio issues ephemeral cert → sign the artifact → log the event to Rekor → discard the private key. Verification: locate the Rekor entry → verify the cert chain → verify the signature. No key material persists after signing.
Sigstore was adopted by PyPI in 2023 for package provenance and by npm (experimental) in 2023. GitHub Artifact Attestations, released in 2024, builds directly on Sigstore infrastructure.

Sigstore makes signing easy by removing the need to manage private keys. You prove who you are via login, get a ten-minute certificate, sign, and throw the key away. The transparency log proves the signature happened and when.

cards.title: Cosign — Signing and Verifying Artifacts
cards.teaser: Cosign is the primary CLI for the Sigstore ecosystem. It signs container images, files, and attestations; verifies them against expected identities; and stores signatures in OCI registries alongside the artifacts they protect.

runs.text: Cosign (github.com/sigstore/cosign) supports two signing modes: keyless (via Sigstore OIDC) and key-based (via a private key you manage). Keyless is the recommended default for CI workflows.
Core operations:

items.text: Sign a container image (keyless, in GitHub Actions):

explanation.text:
# COSIGN_EXPERIMENTAL=1 enables keyless mode
COSIGN_EXPERIMENTAL=1 cosign sign \
  --yes \
  ghcr.io/myorg/myapp@sha256:abc123...

# Generate key pair
cosign generate-key-pair

# Sign
cosign sign --key cosign.key ghcr.io/myorg/myapp:latest

# Verify
cosign verify --key cosign.pub ghcr.io/myorg/myapp:latest

runs.text: Cosign stores signatures as OCI artifacts in the same registry as the image, using the
:sha256-<digest>.sig
tag convention. This means signatures travel with images — no separate signature distribution infrastructure required.
For Kubernetes,
Policy Controller
(formerly Connaisseur) and
Kyverno
can enforce that pods only run images with valid Cosign signatures, blocking unsigned images at admission time.

Cosign is the tool that does the signing and verifying in the Sigstore ecosystem. You sign an image with a GitHub Actions identity, and later you (or your Kubernetes cluster) verify that the image was built by that specific workflow before running it.

cards.title: Provenance Attestations
cards.teaser: A provenance attestation is a signed statement that answers: who built this, from what source, using what process, at what time? The in-toto framework provides the specification; Cosign provides the mechanism to attach and verify it.

runs.text: An
attestation
is a signed, verifiable claim about an artifact. The
in-toto
framework (in-toto.io), developed at NYU, provides the specification for software supply-chain attestations. It defines two key concepts:

items.text: — records what a specific build step did: its inputs (source files, dependencies), its outputs (artifacts), and the command that ran.
— defines the expected supply chain: which steps must occur, in what order, performed by which authorized functionaries (identified by public key).

runs.text: SLSA provenance is a specific in-toto attestation type that records:

items.text: — the URI of the build platform (e.g.,
— the schema describing the build process.
— the source commit SHA and any other inputs consumed.

runs.text: Cosign attaches attestations to OCI artifacts:

explanation.text:
# Attach a SLSA provenance attestation
cosign attest \
  --predicate provenance.json \
  --type slsaprovenance \
  ghcr.io/myorg/myapp@sha256:abc123...

# Verify the attestation
cosign verify-attestation \
  --type slsaprovenance \
  --certificate-identity-regexp "https://github.com/myorg/" \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer "https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com" \
  ghcr.io/myorg/myapp@sha256:abc123...

runs.text: A provenance attestation is a signed receipt: it says this specific artifact was built from this commit, by this CI workflow, at this time. You attach it to the artifact, and anyone who downloads the artifact can verify the receipt was not forged.

cards.title: Dependency Confusion
cards.teaser: Dependency confusion exploits how package managers resolve names: if your private package registry and the public registry share a name, attackers publish a higher-versioned malicious package to the public registry — and the package manager pulls it automatically.

runs.text: Dependency confusion (also called
namespace confusion

) was documented by security researcher Alex Birsan in February 2021. His paper showed that many major companies (Apple, Microsoft, Tesla, Shopify, Uber, Yelp, PayPal) could be attacked by simply uploading a package to the public npm registry with the same name as an internal private package, but with a higher version number.
How it works:

items.text: Company has an internal package named
at version 1.2.3 in a private registry.
at version 9.9.9 to the public npm registry.
The package manager, configured to check both registries, sees the public version 9.9.9 is "newer" than the private 1.2.3 and installs the public (malicious) version.
The malicious package's install script executes during
, exfiltrating data from the CI environment or developer machine.

runs.text: Mitigations:

items.text: registered publicly as an empty placeholder).
— configure the package manager to resolve internal packages only from the private registry (npmrc
— a committed lockfile pins exact versions and registry origins, preventing unexpected resolution of newer public versions.
— publish placeholder packages to public registries under your internal names, preventing adversarial occupation.

runs.text: If your internal package is named the same as a public one, an attacker can publish a higher-versioned malicious copy publicly and your package manager will download it automatically. The fix is to use scoped names and tell your package manager exactly which registry to use for internal packages.

cards.title: Typosquatting — Malicious Look-alike Packages
cards.teaser: Typosquatting exploits the gap between what a developer meant to type and what they actually typed. attackers register package names that are one character away from popular libraries and wait for the installs to roll in.

runs.text: Typosquatting is the registration of a package name that is a typographic variant of a popular legitimate package. The attacker does nothing after publishing — they wait for developers to mistype a package name during installation.
Common typosquatting techniques:

items.text: . This exact attack was executed in 2021 and downloaded 12,000 times before removal.
(PyPI normalizes these, but npm does not).
— legitimate name with an appended word:

runs.text: Notable typosquatting incidents on PyPI and npm number in the hundreds. In 2022, researchers found over 200 malicious PyPI packages in a single campaign targeting AWS credentials and Discord tokens.
Mitigations:

items.text: — once the correct package is installed, a lockfile prevents accidental typo-driven reinstallation.
— check download counts, repository links, and maintainer profiles before adding a new dependency.
— private artifact proxies (Artifactory, Nexus) can allowlist approved packages, blocking any unlisted package installation.

runs.text: Typosquatting is simply registering a package name one typo away from a famous package, then sitting back and collecting installs from developers who mistype. The defense is lockfiles, scrutiny before adding packages, and a private proxy that only allows approved names.

cards.title: Malicious Package Techniques
cards.teaser: Malicious packages rarely hide in obvious places. They execute during installation via lifecycle hooks, phone home via obfuscated network calls, or lie dormant until a specific triggering condition is met at runtime.

runs.text: Once an attacker has a package installed, they use several techniques to execute malicious code:

items.text: with no additional user confirmation. The event-stream attack (2018) used a postinstall script; most credential-stealing npm attacks use this vector. Python's
runs at install time and is equally exploitable.
— the package appears functional but exfiltrates data during normal operation. Malicious packages have been found that steal environment variables (containing API keys) on every process startup.
— the initial package is clean, but a postinstall script downloads and executes a second-stage payload from a remote server. This technique evades static analysis at publication time.

— the malicious code only activates under specific conditions: a specific hostname, a specific environment variable, or after detecting a target application. The event-stream attack only activated in the Copay Bitcoin wallet context.

— legitimate packages are backdoored by taking over a maintainer's account (credential stuffing, phishing, or a leaked token). The ua-parser-js npm package (8M weekly downloads) was compromised this way in 2021.

runs.text: Use npm install --ignore-scripts to suppress lifecycle hook execution for untrusted packages. In CI environments, consider using --foreground-scripts to make script execution visible in logs. Python equivalent: pip install --no-build-isolation.

Malicious packages usually strike during installation via hooks that run automatically, not while your app is running. They steal environment variables, download a second payload, or lie dormant until they detect a specific target. The best defense is to never blindly run install scripts and to pin your dependencies.

cards.title: Build Attestations and GitHub OIDC
cards.teaser: GitHub OIDC tokens give CI jobs a cryptographically verifiable identity without storing long-lived secrets. Combined with build attestations, they allow you to prove that a specific artifact was built by a specific workflow on a specific commit.

runs.text: A
build attestation
is a signed statement about a build: who ran it, what source it consumed, and what artifact it produced. GitHub OIDC (OpenID Connect) provides the identity infrastructure.
How GitHub OIDC works in CI:

items.text: The GitHub Actions runner requests a short-lived OIDC token from GitHub's token endpoint.
The token is a JWT containing claims: the repository name, the workflow path, the git ref, the commit SHA, the triggering event, and the run ID. These claims are signed by GitHub's private key.
The token can be exchanged with Fulcio (Sigstore's CA) for a code-signing certificate. The certificate contains the workflow identity as the subject.
When you sign an artifact with this certificate, the signature carries the full workflow identity as metadata.

runs.text: GitHub Artifact Attestations (2024) wraps this into a single command:

explanation.text:
- name: Generate attestation
  uses: actions/attest-build-provenance@v1
  with:
    subject-name: ghcr.io/myorg/myapp
    subject-digest: ${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}

runs.text: Verification:

OIDC-based signing eliminates the need to store AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, DOCKER_PASSWORD, or other long-lived credentials in GitHub Secrets for deployment purposes. The same mechanism works with AWS, GCP, and Azure — each accepts GitHub OIDC tokens for workload identity federation.

GitHub OIDC gives your CI job a provable identity — like a passport — that lasts only for that one run. You use that identity to sign your artifact, and anyone verifying it later can confirm the exact workflow, repository, and commit that produced it.

cards.title: Defending the Supply Chain
cards.teaser: No single control secures the software supply chain. Defense in depth means lockfiles, integrity hashes, signed commits, dependency scanning, SBOM generation, and reproducible builds working together as a system.

runs.text: A practical supply-chain defense program combines controls at every layer:

items.text: to the repository. A lockfile pins exact versions and, in npm's case, integrity hashes, preventing version drift and ensuring reproducible installs.
— npm's Subresource Integrity (SRI) hashes in the lockfile verify that the installed content matches what was originally resolved. Python's
enforces SHA-256 verification for every package.

— GPG or SSH-signed commits verify committer identity. Combined with branch protection rules requiring signed commits, they prevent unauthorized code injection into the repository. Required for SLSA Level 4.

— Dependabot, Renovate, and Snyk continuously monitor dependencies against CVE databases and open pull requests for vulnerable versions. Automation here is critical: manual vulnerability triage does not scale.

— route all package downloads through an Artifactory or Nexus instance with an approved-packages allowlist. Blocks typosquatting and dependency confusion by preventing unapproved packages from reaching developers and CI.
— generate and store an SBOM as a CI artifact. Feed it to a vulnerability database (Dependency-Track, Grype) for continuous monitoring.

— ensure that building from the same source produces bit-for-bit identical output. Reproducibility eliminates an entire class of build-pipeline compromise: if the artifact does not match what independent builds produce, it was tampered with.
— restrict CI jobs to the minimum required permissions. A build job does not need write access to the production environment. A test job should not have access to production secrets.

runs.text: The xz-utils attack was stopped by accident, not by any of these controls. Reproducible builds would have detected the discrepancy between source and distributed tarballs — the attacker modified the build system, not the tracked source. This illustrates why build process integrity (SLSA Level 3+) matters independently of source integrity.

Supply-chain defense is layered: lockfiles prevent version drift, hashes catch tampered downloads, signed commits verify authors, dependency scanners catch known vulnerabilities, and SBOM generation makes the entire component inventory auditable. No single control is sufficient; all of them working together raise the cost of attack dramatically.

cards.title: The Trust Model of Package Ecosystems
cards.teaser: npm, PyPI, and Maven Central operate on a publish-and-trust model — anyone can publish, and consumers assume published packages are safe. Understanding the trust model's weaknesses is the prerequisite for layering compensating controls.

runs.text: Public package registries were not designed with adversarial publishers in mind. Their trust model has several structural weaknesses:

items.text: — anyone with an email address can publish to npm or PyPI. There is no verification that "Facebook" the publisher is actually Meta.

— package ownership can be transferred to a new maintainer without consumer notification. The event-stream npm attack exploited this: the original maintainer transferred ownership to an attacker claiming to want to help maintain the package.
No malware scanning at publish time

— registries run basic checks but do not perform deep static analysis. Malicious packages frequently survive initial publication and are removed only after researchers or automated scanners detect them post-publication.

— a single direct dependency can pull in dozens of transitive dependencies, each with its own maintainers and risk profile. Most organizations audit their direct dependencies but not their transitive graph.

runs.text: Registry improvements underway:

items.text: — requires 2FA for high-impact packages (1M+ weekly downloads) since 2022. Sigstore-based provenance attestations since 2023.
— mandates 2FA for top-8,000 packages (by download) since 2023. Trusted Publishers (OIDC-based publishing from GitHub Actions) eliminates PyPI tokens in CI since 2023.
— requires GPG-signed artifacts and namespace verification (domain ownership proof) for new publisher registrations since 2024.

runs.text: Public package registries default to trusting publishers — anyone can publish, and no one verifies that the publisher is who they claim to be. The registries are improving, but the baseline trust model means consumers must add their own controls rather than relying on the registry to catch everything.

cards.title: Reproducible Builds
cards.teaser: A reproducible build produces bit-for-bit identical output from identical inputs. Reproducibility transforms the question 'do I trust this artifact?' into a verifiable, auditable property — and it is the basis of SLSA Level 4.

runs.text: Most build processes are not reproducible by default. Timestamps, random seeds, non-deterministic linking, and tool-version differences cause the same source to produce different binaries on different machines or at different times. This non-determinism creates an untestable gap between source and artifact.
Common sources of build non-determinism:

items.text: — file modification times embedded in archives. Fix: use
(a standardized environment variable respected by many build tools to normalize timestamps to a fixed value).
— filesystem traversal order varies. Fix: sort file lists explicitly before processing.
— compilers embed the absolute path of the build directory. Fix: use
— different compiler or linker versions produce different output. Fix: pin tool versions in Dockerfiles or Nix environments.

runs.text: The
reproducible-builds.org
project has been working since 2013 to make Debian, Arch Linux, and other distributions reproducible. Their tooling (
diffoscope
) identifies sources of non-determinism by comparing two builds side-by-side.

Security value: if an attacker compromises the build pipeline and modifies a binary, independent rebuilds will produce different output. Independent verification of the build — rebuilding from source and comparing digests — becomes a meaningful security check only if the build is reproducible.

The xz-utils backdoor was inserted into the distributed tarball but not into the git repository source. A reproducible build — building from git source and comparing to the distributed tarball — would have detected the discrepancy immediately.

Reproducible builds mean anyone can rebuild your software from source and get the exact same binary. That makes tampering detectable: if the official binary does not match the independent rebuild, something in the pipeline modified it. Without reproducibility, you cannot tell.
